The physiotherapy approach prioritizes pacing, energy conservation, gradual activity progression below symptom threshold, and monitoring SpO2 during activity. HIIT risks PEM exacerbation.

question_text: For the teacher with MS described above, which fatigue management strategy BEST addresses her pattern of worsening fatigue by mid-afternoon?
option_a: Schedule the most cognitively and physically demanding teaching tasks in the morning when energy is highest, and plan a rest period during lunch
option_b: Recommend she takes a full sick leave from teaching until fatigue resolves completely
option_c: Prescribe high-intensity aerobic exercise every afternoon to combat fatigue
option_d: Advise her to drink caffeinated beverages throughout the day to maintain alertness
rationale: Energy conservation in MS-related fatigue involves pacing and prioritizing high-demand tasks during peak energy windows. For this teacher, mornings represent her best energy period. A structured rest at lunch and front-loading demanding tasks is the evidence-based fatigue management approach (energy conservation strategy). Sick leave, high-intensity PM exercise, or caffeine dependence are not appropriate primary strategies.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 34-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis experienced a relapse 6 weeks ago affecting her right leg. She has been discharged from hospital on a short course of IV methylprednisolone. Current deficits: right leg weakness (hip flexors 3+/5, knee extensors 4/5), fatigue (MFIS score 52/84), heat sensitivity (Uhthoff's phenomenon), EDSS 4.0. She works as a teacher and reports her fatigue worsens significantly by mid-afternoon.

question_text: Given this patient's Uhthoff's phenomenon, which exercise environment modification is MOST important to implement?
option_a: Ensure the exercise space is well-lit to prevent visual disturbances during activity
option_b: Exercise in a cool environment (ideally 16–20°C) and use cooling vests or cool water immersion before and during exercise
option_c: Avoid all aerobic exercise permanently, as heat will permanently worsen her MS
option_d: Schedule exercise only in the evening when outdoor temperatures are cooler
rationale: Uhthoff's phenomenon is a transient worsening of MS symptoms with elevated core body temperature. Exercise in a cool environment and use of pre-cooling strategies (cooling vests, cool water) are evidence-based interventions to allow safe participation in exercise. Symptoms are transient, not permanent, so avoiding all exercise is incorrect. Evening timing alone is insufficient.

question_text: An EDSS score of 4.0 in this patient indicates which functional status?
option_a: Fully ambulatory without limitation, with minimal disability in one functional system
option_b: Ambulatory without aid for at least 500 meters but with significant disability limiting full daily activity
option_c: Requires unilateral assistance (cane) to walk 100 meters
option_d: Restricted to a wheelchair for most of the day
rationale: EDSS 4.0 indicates the patient is fully ambulatory without aid for at least 500 meters but has relatively severe disability in multiple functional systems, enough to impair full daily activities. EDSS 5.0 is when ambulation is limited to ~200m without aid. EDSS 6.0 requires unilateral assistance. EDSS 7.0+ involves wheelchair dependence.

question_text: For this burn patient with hypertrophic scarring risk, when should compression garment therapy be initiated?
option_a: Immediately after the burn injury, before any surgical intervention
option_b: Once graft sites and donor sites are fully healed (≥95% epithelialization), typically 2–3 weeks post-grafting
option_c: Only after the scar has matured completely, which takes 12–18 months
option_d: Compression garments should not be used in the presence of skin grafts
rationale: Compression garment therapy for hypertrophic scar prevention is initiated once wounds are sufficiently healed — typically when ≥95% epithelialization has occurred. Starting too early risks wound breakdown, while waiting until full maturation misses the critical prevention window. Grafted areas can tolerate compression once the graft is stable and donor sites are closed.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 29-year-old male sustained burns in a house fire 2 weeks ago. Total body surface area involved: 25% (anterior trunk, bilateral upper arms). Depth: mixed deep partial thickness and full thickness. He has undergone split-thickness skin grafting to the full-thickness areas 10 days ago. The graft sites are healing. He has significant pruritus and tightness across the chest. Occupational PT assessment shows reduced shoulder flexion bilaterally (right 110°, left 95°) due to developing hypertrophic scarring.

question_text: For this patient with anterior chest burns and developing shoulder restriction, what is the MOST appropriate anti-contracture splinting position?
option_a: Shoulder adduction and internal rotation with elbow flexion to protect the healing grafts
option_b: Shoulder abduction (80–90°) and external rotation with elbow extension to oppose the contracture forces on the anterior chest
option_c: Bilateral shoulder elevation in full flexion (180°) with cervical flexion
option_d: Neutral shoulder position with no splinting, relying only on exercise
rationale: Anti-contracture positioning for anterior chest and axillary burns places the shoulder in abduction (80–90°) and external rotation with elbow extension. This opposes the flexion and adduction contracture forces that develop with anterior chest scarring. Adduction and internal rotation would encourage contracture formation, which is the opposite of the therapeutic goal.

question_text: Using the Rule of Nines, how is this patient's 25% TBSA burn distribution MOST accurately calculated from the described areas?
option_a: Anterior trunk (18%) + bilateral upper arms (9% total) = 27%, rounded down to 25% with partial involvement
option_b: Anterior trunk (9%) + bilateral upper arms (9% each = 18%) = 27%, adjusted to 25%
option_c: Anterior trunk (18%) + each upper arm (4% each = 8%) = 26%, consistent with 25% estimate given partial involvement
option_d: Entire trunk front and back (36%) divided by the uninvolved back = 25%
rationale: By the Rule of Nines, the anterior trunk = 18%, and each entire arm = 9% (upper arm ~4%, forearm ~3%, hand ~2%). Anterior trunk (18%) + bilateral upper arms (~4% each = 8%) = 26%, which is consistent with the reported 25% given that not all surfaces were uniformly involved. Option A incorrectly assigns 9% to both upper arms combined.

question_text: For this 6-week postpartum woman with pelvic floor strength of 2/5 and 2-second holds, what is the MOST appropriate initial pelvic floor exercise prescription?
option_a: Maximum effort Kegel contractions held for 10 seconds, 30 repetitions, 3 times daily
option_b: Short-duration submaximal contractions (2–3 second holds), 8–12 repetitions, 3 sets, with rest intervals, progressed as endurance improves
option_c: Heavy resistance exercises including weighted squats immediately to maximize recruitment
option_d: No pelvic floor exercises until 12 weeks postpartum to allow full tissue healing
rationale: With a 2/5 pelvic floor strength and 2-second endurance, the initial prescription should match current capacity — short submaximal holds, 8–12 reps, 3 sets with rest. Progressing prematurely to 10-second holds when she can only sustain 2 seconds leads to compensatory strategies and fatigue without effective muscle training. Exercises can begin safely at 6 weeks postpartum.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 31-year-old woman is referred to pelvic floor physiotherapy 6 weeks postpartum following a vaginal delivery with a second-degree perineal laceration. She reports stress urinary incontinence (leaking with coughing, sneezing, and running) and pelvic heaviness at end of day. She is breastfeeding. Pelvic floor muscle assessment (internal exam): pelvic floor strength 2/5 (Modified Oxford Scale), poor endurance (holds 2 seconds), diastasis recti 2.5 cm at the umbilicus.

question_text: A diastasis recti measurement of 2.5 cm at the umbilicus in this postpartum woman is clinically significant because:
option_a: It indicates a hernia requiring immediate surgical repair before any physiotherapy can proceed
option_b: It exceeds the commonly cited threshold of 2.0 cm (or >2 finger-widths), suggesting impaired linea alba function and need for exercise modification to avoid increasing intra-abdominal pressure
option_c: It is within normal limits for a postpartum woman and requires no clinical consideration
option_d: It indicates the pelvic floor is not involved and stress incontinence must have another cause
rationale: A diastasis recti >2.0 cm (approximately 2 finger-widths) at the umbilicus is clinically significant. It indicates reduced linea alba tension, which affects load transfer and intra-abdominal pressure management. Exercise prescription must be modified to avoid exercises that increase intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., sit-ups, double leg raises) until function improves. Surgery is not indicated initially.

question_text: Why might breastfeeding affect this patient's pelvic floor rehabilitation progress?
option_a: Breastfeeding causes excessive weight loss that weakens all muscles equally
option_b: Breastfeeding maintains elevated prolactin and reduces estrogen levels, leading to tissue hypoestrogenism that reduces pelvic floor tissue elasticity and may worsen vaginal atrophy and urinary symptoms
option_c: Breastfeeding increases estrogen which causes pelvic floor muscle hypertrophy and over-activity
option_d: Breastfeeding has no hormonal effect on pelvic floor rehabilitation
rationale: During breastfeeding, elevated prolactin suppresses ovarian estrogen production. This hypoestrogenic state reduces tissue collagen content and elasticity, and is associated with vaginal atrophy, mucosal changes, and potentially worsened stress urinary incontinence. This is an important clinical consideration when setting expectations for pelvic floor rehab progress in breastfeeding patients.

question_text: For this 74-year-old with EF 25% and CRT-D programmed to 130 bpm upper rate, what is the MOST appropriate exercise intensity prescription?
option_a: Target heart rate 60–70% of age-predicted maximum (HRmax = 220 – 74 = 146 bpm; target 88–102 bpm)
option_b: Use RPE scale (Borg 11–13, 'light to somewhat hard') as the primary intensity guide, keeping HR well below the CRT-D upper rate limit of 130 bpm
option_c: High-intensity interval training at 85–95% HRmax for maximum cardiac adaptation
option_d: No aerobic exercise; only passive range of motion due to low ejection fraction
rationale: In patients with CRT-D devices and severely reduced EF (25%), RPE-based prescription (Borg 11–13) is preferred because heart rate response may be blunted by beta-blockers and the device. Exercise intensity must remain below the device's upper rate limit (130 bpm) to avoid triggering device therapy. High-intensity exercise and passive-only approaches are both inappropriate for cardiac rehab in stable heart failure.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 74-year-old male with ischemic cardiomyopathy, ejection fraction 25%, NYHA Class III heart failure, is referred to a supervised hospital-based cardiac rehabilitation program. His most recent 6MWT: 195m (predicted 520m for his age). He has a cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator (CRT-D) with upper rate limit programmed at 130 bpm. Resting vitals: HR 68, BP 102/68, SpO2 96%. He is on optimal medical therapy including ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, and spironolactone.

question_text: What is the PRIMARY significance of a CRT-D upper rate limit of 130 bpm for exercise prescription in this patient?
option_a: The device will automatically pace the heart at 130 bpm throughout all exercise sessions
option_b: If the patient's heart rate reaches 130 bpm, the device may deliver a shock, so exercise intensity must keep HR reliably below this limit
option_c: The 130 bpm limit means the patient can safely exercise up to 130 bpm without any monitoring
option_d: The upper rate limit is irrelevant because beta-blockers will prevent the HR from rising above 100 bpm
rationale: ICD/CRT-D devices have a programmed upper detection rate. If the patient's HR reaches or exceeds the therapy zone threshold, the device may incorrectly interpret the rhythm as a tachyarrhythmia and deliver an inappropriate shock. Exercise intensity must be prescribed to keep HR safely (typically 10–15 bpm) below this upper limit. While beta-blockers do blunt HR response, relying solely on this is insufficient.

question_text: Which of the following is an absolute indication to STOP exercise immediately in this patient during a cardiac rehab session?
option_a: Heart rate increases from 68 to 95 bpm during warm-up
option_b: Systolic blood pressure drops 10 mmHg below resting value during exercise progression
option_c: Patient reports mild leg fatigue (RPE 12) at 10 minutes
option_d: Respiratory rate increases to 22 breaths/min during moderate exercise
rationale: An exertional drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mmHg below resting SBP) during exercise is an absolute contraindication to continuing exercise. It signals hemodynamic instability — in severe heart failure with EF 25%, this can indicate worsening cardiac output, impending hemodynamic collapse, or significant arrhythmia. HR increase, mild fatigue, and mild tachypnea are expected physiological responses.

question_text: In this 13-year-old with Risser Stage 2, what does this staging indicate regarding growth remaining and curve progression risk?
option_a: Risser Stage 2 indicates skeletal maturity is nearly complete, with minimal growth remaining and low curve progression risk
option_b: Risser Stage 2 (approximately 50% iliac apophysis ossification) indicates significant growth remaining, placing her at HIGH risk of curve progression and making bracing appropriate
option_c: Risser Stage 2 indicates the patient has completed her adolescent growth spurt with no further scoliosis risk
option_d: Risser Stage 2 indicates surgery should be performed immediately to prevent further progression
rationale: The Risser sign grades iliac apophysis ossification from 0 (no ossification, most growth remaining) to 5 (complete fusion, skeletal maturity). Stage 2 (~50% ossification) indicates the patient still has substantial growth remaining, making her at significant risk for curve progression. This, combined with a 32° Cobb angle, places her firmly in the bracing indication range.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 13-year-old girl is referred to PT with a diagnosis of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Standing X-ray: right thoracic curve Cobb angle 32°, left lumbar compensatory curve 18°. Risser sign: Stage 2 (approximately 50% iliac apophysis ossification). Her family is concerned about curve progression and asks about bracing versus observation. She has no pain and no neurological symptoms. Her physiatrist has prescribed a TLSO brace.

question_text: According to current evidence-based guidelines for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, at what Cobb angle is bracing typically indicated versus observation versus surgical referral?
option_a: Observation: <10°; Bracing: 10–20°; Surgery: >20°
option_b: Observation: <25°; Bracing: 25–45° in skeletally immature patients; Surgery: >45–50°
option_c: Bracing is indicated for all curves regardless of Cobb angle in skeletally immature patients
option_d: Observation: <40°; Bracing: 40–55°; Surgery: >55°
rationale: Current AIS management guidelines: Observation for curves <25° (or <20° with close monitoring); Bracing for curves 25–45° in skeletally immature patients (Risser 0–2) to prevent progression; Surgical referral for curves >45–50° or rapidly progressing curves. This patient (32°, Risser 2) appropriately falls in the bracing range. The BrAIST study confirmed brace efficacy in preventing progression.

question_text: The Schroth method for AIS — what is it and what does current evidence show?
option_a: A surgical technique for spinal fusion using Cobb angle correction; evidence shows it replaces bracing effectively
option_b: A three-dimensional scoliosis-specific exercise approach using postural correction, muscle activation, and breathing techniques; evidence shows it can reduce Cobb angle progression and improve posture and quality of life as an adjunct to or alternative to bracing in mild-moderate curves
option_c: A hydrotherapy-based approach with no evidence of clinical benefit for scoliosis curves
option_d: A passive manual therapy technique requiring no patient participation; evidence shows it permanently corrects curves >30°
rationale: The Schroth method is a scoliosis-specific physiotherapy exercise approach developed in Germany, focusing on 3D postural correction, elongation, derotation, and stabilization using scoliosis-specific breathing (rotational angular breathing). Evidence (including RCTs) shows benefit in reducing curve progression and improving Cobb angle, trunk rotation, and quality of life. It is recommended as an adjunct to bracing in moderate curves per SOSORT guidelines.

question_text: A 45-year-old construction worker presents with a 3-week history of low back pain radiating to the left leg in an L5 distribution (dorsum of foot, big toe). Which finding would MOST strongly suggest lumbar disc herniation at L4-L5?
option_a: Absent ankle reflex on the left side
option_b: Weakness of extensor hallucis longus (EHL) and foot dorsiflexors on the left, positive SLR at 40° reproducing leg pain
option_c: Reduced sensation in the S1 dermatome (lateral foot) and weak plantar flexion
option_d: Positive Trendelenburg sign and groin pain
rationale: L5 nerve root compression (from L4-L5 disc herniation) causes weakness of EHL and dorsiflexors, reduced sensation over the dorsum of the foot and big toe, and positive SLR reproducing leg pain. Absent ankle reflex and plantar flexion weakness are S1 signs (L5-S1 level). Trendelenburg and groin pain suggest hip pathology.

question_text: Which special test for shoulder impingement has the HIGHEST sensitivity and is therefore MOST useful for RULING OUT supraspinatus impingement when negative?
option_a: Hawkins-Kennedy test
option_b: Neer impingement sign
option_c: Empty Can (Jobe) test
option_d: Drop Arm test
rationale: The Hawkins-Kennedy test has reported sensitivity of ~79–92% for supraspinatus impingement, making it one of the most sensitive tests for ruling out impingement when negative (high sensitivity = good rule-out test, SnNout). The Neer sign is also sensitive (~72–88%). The Empty Can and Drop Arm tests are more specific for rotator cuff tears rather than impingement.

question_text: A 22-year-old recreational soccer player presents 3 days post-ACL reconstruction (bone-patellar tendon-bone graft). Which immediate post-operative goal is MOST critical in the first 2 weeks?
option_a: Return to sport-specific agility training
option_b: Full knee extension range of motion (ROM) and quadriceps activation (quad sets, SLR)
option_c: Progressive resistance leg press to 80% 1RM
option_d: Deep water running at maximum effort
rationale: In the first 2 weeks post-ACL reconstruction, the priority goals are: (1) achieving full knee extension to prevent flexion contracture, and (2) early quadriceps activation (quad sets, SLR) to prevent quadriceps inhibition and atrophy. Extension loss is the most common post-operative complication and is very difficult to correct later. High-load exercises and agility training are contraindicated at this stage.

question_text: A 60-year-old woman is diagnosed with adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) in the 'frozen phase.' Which physical therapy approach is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Aggressive manipulation under anesthesia immediately to restore ROM
option_b: Joint mobilizations (Grade III-IV), stretching, and patient education about the natural history; goal is symptom management and gradual ROM restoration
option_c: Surgical release is the first-line treatment in the frozen phase
option_d: Complete rest and immobilization to allow the capsule to heal
rationale: In the frozen phase of adhesive capsulitis, physical therapy with Grade III-IV joint mobilizations, stretching (particularly inferior capsule and posterior capsule), and patient education is appropriate. The condition is largely self-limiting (18–24 months natural history). Aggressive MUA has variable evidence and risks. Rest and immobilization worsen the condition. Surgery is reserved for recalcitrant cases.

question_text: The Ottawa Ankle Rules indicate an ankle X-ray is required if a patient has pain in the malleolar zone AND:
option_a: Tenderness anywhere along the distal fibula or tibia
option_b: Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral or medial malleolus (6 cm), OR inability to bear weight immediately and in the emergency department (4 steps)
option_c: Any swelling around the ankle joint
option_d: Tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament only
rationale: The Ottawa Ankle Rules require X-ray if there is malleolar zone pain AND: bone tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of either malleolus within 6 cm, OR inability to weight-bear for 4 steps (immediately and in the ED). General swelling or ATFL tenderness alone does not meet criteria. These rules have >96% sensitivity for fracture detection.

question_text: A 55-year-old office worker presents with lateral elbow pain for 4 months consistent with lateral epicondylalgia. Which exercise approach has the STRONGEST evidence for long-term outcomes?
option_a: Passive modalities only (ultrasound, TENS) without exercise
option_b: Progressive wrist extensor eccentric and heavy slow resistance (HSR) loading exercises
option_c: Complete rest from all activities involving the wrist and elbow
option_d: Corticosteroid injection repeated monthly for 6 months
rationale: For lateral epicondylalgia (formerly 'tennis elbow'), progressive loading exercises — including eccentric and heavy slow resistance (HSR) protocols for wrist extensors — have the strongest long-term evidence. Studies (including Stasinopoulos et al.) show superior outcomes at 6–12 months compared to passive treatment, injection, or rest. Repeated corticosteroid injections show short-term relief but worse long-term outcomes than exercise.

question_text: A 68-year-old man 6 months post-right MCA stroke has left hemiplegia. He has recovered to Brunnstrom Stage 4 in his left arm. What does Brunnstrom Stage 4 indicate?
option_a: No voluntary movement possible
option_b: Spasticity beginning to appear with basic limb synergies
option_c: Some voluntary movement outside synergy patterns beginning to emerge, spasticity declining
option_d: Near-normal voluntary movement with minimal synergy influence
rationale: Brunnstrom Stage 4 is characterized by emergence of some voluntary movement combinations outside of the obligatory flexion/extension synergy patterns, with declining spasticity. Stage 1 = flaccidity, Stage 2 = synergies emerging, Stage 3 = peak synergy control, Stage 4 = some deviation from synergy, Stage 5 = largely independent of synergy, Stage 6 = near-normal coordination.

question_text: A 72-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease falls frequently. Which physiotherapy intervention has the STRONGEST evidence for fall reduction in Parkinson's disease?
option_a: Passive stretching twice weekly
option_b: Treadmill training with rhythmic auditory cueing, combined with balance training
option_c: Bed rest to prevent falls
option_d: Strengthening of hip abductors only
rationale: In Parkinson's disease, exercise programs combining treadmill or rhythmic auditory cueing with balance training have the strongest evidence for fall reduction. Rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) leverages preserved external cueing to bypass the defective internal timing circuits in PD. Balance and gait training specifically targeting PD pathophysiology (freezing, festination) are most effective.

question_text: A patient presents with foot drop after a common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular head. Which orthosis is MOST appropriate for ambulation?
option_a: Knee-ankle-foot orthosis (KAFO) to stabilize the entire lower limb
option_b: Posterior leaf spring ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) to assist dorsiflexion during swing phase
option_c: Rigid ankle fusion brace in plantar flexion
option_d: Lateral wedge insole only
rationale: Common peroneal nerve injury causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion). A posterior leaf spring AFO is the standard orthotic intervention, providing passive dorsiflexion assistance during swing phase to clear the foot and prevent tripping. A KAFO is more appropriate for quadriceps weakness. Plantar flexion positioning would worsen the deficit.

question_text: Which outcome measure is MOST appropriate to assess dynamic balance and fall risk in community-dwelling older adults with neurological conditions?
option_a: Manual Muscle Testing (MMT)
option_b: The Berg Balance Scale (BBS)
option_c: The Oswestry Disability Index (ODI)
option_d: The 10-meter walk test for speed only
rationale: The Berg Balance Scale (BBS) is a validated 14-item clinical balance assessment tool widely used in older adults and neurological populations. A score <45/56 identifies elevated fall risk. It assesses static and dynamic balance tasks relevant to daily function. The ODI is for low back pain; MMT measures strength, not balance; the 10MWT measures gait speed but not balance.

question_text: A 58-year-old post-CABG patient is in Phase II cardiac rehabilitation. His resting HR is 55 bpm (on metoprolol). Which method is MOST appropriate for prescribing aerobic exercise intensity?
option_a: Age-predicted HRmax formula (220 – age) × 65–85%
option_b: Heart Rate Reserve method (Karvonen formula) using actual resting and measured peak HR
option_c: Fixed HR of 100 bpm for all sessions
option_d: RPE 6–8 on the Borg 6–20 scale ('very light')
rationale: In cardiac rehab patients on beta-blockers, the Karvonen (HRR) method using actual measured HRmax (from ETT or functional test) and actual resting HR is preferred over age-predicted formulas. Beta-blockers blunt the HR response, making age-predicted formulas unreliable. Target: HRR 40–70% (moderate intensity). RPE 6–8 is too light for cardiac conditioning.

question_text: A patient with COPD GOLD Stage III (severe) has an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.58 and FEV1 32% predicted. Which pulmonary rehabilitation component MOST directly reduces dynamic hyperinflation during exercise?
option_a: High-flow supplemental oxygen during all activities
option_b: Pursed-lip breathing and paced breathing techniques to slow respiratory rate and allow more complete exhalation
option_c: Incentive spirometry 10 times per hour
option_d: Postural drainage in the Trendelenburg position
rationale: Dynamic hyperinflation in COPD occurs when expiratory flow limitation prevents complete exhalation before the next breath, progressively increasing end-expiratory lung volume. Pursed-lip breathing reduces respiratory rate, prolongs exhalation time, maintains positive airway pressure to stent open airways, and allows more complete gas emptying — directly reducing dynamic hyperinflation and dyspnea during exercise.

question_text: Which finding during a graded exercise test is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to continuing exercise according to ACSM guidelines?
option_a: Heart rate increase of 20 bpm from resting with moderate exercise
option_b: Drop in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg from a previously established point despite increasing workload, with evidence of ischemia
option_c: Patient reporting mild leg fatigue at stage 2 of the Bruce protocol
option_d: SpO2 decreasing from 98% to 96% during exercise
rationale: ACSM absolute indications to stop exercise testing include: drop in systolic BP >10 mmHg from baseline despite increasing workload (with other signs of ischemia), significant ST changes, serious arrhythmias, signs/symptoms of severe ischemia, technical inability to monitor ECG, subject's desire to stop, and more. Mild fatigue, normal HR increase, or mild SpO2 drop alone are not absolute termination criteria.

question_text: A 40-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis requires airway clearance. Which technique is considered MOST effective for independent long-term airway clearance in CF?
option_a: Postural drainage with manual percussion by a caregiver, performed 4 times daily
option_b: Active Cycle of Breathing Technique (ACBT) or Oscillating PEP (e.g., Flutter, Aerobika), which are self-administered and have equivalent efficacy to conventional chest physiotherapy
option_c: Forced expiratory technique (huffing) alone without any other components
option_d: Incentive spirometry exclusively
rationale: ACBT and oscillating PEP devices (Flutter, Acapella, Aerobika) are self-administered airway clearance techniques with evidence of equivalent efficacy to conventional manual chest physiotherapy (postural drainage with percussion) in CF. They promote independence and are preferred for long-term management. Huffing alone (FET) is one component of ACBT. Incentive spirometry does not clear secretions effectively.

question_text: A 66-year-old man is 4 days post-pneumonectomy (right side) for lung cancer. Which positioning consideration is MOST important for optimizing gas exchange?
option_a: Position with the operative (right) side DOWN to promote drainage and maximize remaining left lung ventilation
option_b: Supine positioning exclusively for 48 hours post-op
option_c: Position with the remaining (left) lung DOWN to maximize perfusion to the functioning lung
option_d: Trendelenburg position for 6 hours daily to drain the pneumonectomy space
rationale: After pneumonectomy, the operative side should be positioned DOWN. This allows the remaining functional lung to be uppermost, where it receives more ventilation relative to perfusion (improved V/Q matching in the remaining lung). Gravity-dependent perfusion to the remaining upper lung is acceptable, and this position also helps prevent mediastinal shift toward the operative side. The opposite positioning would compromise the remaining lung.

question_text: A 70-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presents with a non-healing plantar ulcer on her right great toe. The wound bed shows 80% yellow slough. Which wound debridement method is MOST appropriate in this context?
option_a: Sharp/surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue in a single aggressive session
option_b: Autolytic debridement using a moisture-retentive dressing (hydrogel or hydrocolloid) over several weeks, combined with off-loading
option_c: Wet-to-dry dressing changes three times daily
option_d: No debridement; cover with dry gauze and monitor
rationale: For a diabetic plantar ulcer with slough, autolytic debridement with moisture-retentive dressings (hydrogels for dry wounds, hydrocolloids for moist) is generally appropriate as a conservative first approach, combined with pressure off-loading. Aggressive sharp debridement may be indicated in infected or devitalized tissue but carries risk in poorly perfused diabetic feet. Wet-to-dry dressings are non-selective and damage granulation tissue.

question_text: In pressure injury staging, a Stage 3 pressure injury is characterized by:
option_a: Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin
option_b: Partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis, moist wound bed, no fascia visible
option_c: Full-thickness tissue loss with visible subcutaneous fat, but no exposed tendon, bone, or muscle
option_d: Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle
rationale: NPUAP/EPUAP staging: Stage 1 = non-blanchable erythema of intact skin; Stage 2 = partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis; Stage 3 = full-thickness tissue loss with visible subcutaneous fat (but no exposed bone/tendon/muscle); Stage 4 = full-thickness with exposed bone, tendon, or muscle. Unstageable = full-thickness with obscured base.

question_text: A patient with a venous leg ulcer has an ABI (ankle-brachial index) of 0.85. Which compression therapy is MOST appropriate?
option_a: No compression is permitted with ABI <0.9
option_b: High compression (40 mmHg at ankle) four-layer bandage system
option_c: Reduced/modified compression (23–30 mmHg) with close monitoring, as ABI 0.8–0.9 allows cautious compression
option_d: Surgical referral is the only appropriate next step
rationale: ABI interpretation for compression: >0.9 = normal arterial supply, full compression appropriate; 0.8–0.9 = mild-moderate arterial disease, modified/reduced compression (23–30 mmHg) is generally acceptable with monitoring; 0.5–0.8 = significant arterial disease, compression contraindicated or very cautious; <0.5 = critical ischemia, compression contraindicated. This patient (ABI 0.85) can receive cautious reduced compression.

question_text: A 78-year-old woman is assessed using the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test and completes it in 16 seconds. What does this result indicate?
option_a: Normal functional mobility; no fall risk
option_b: Moderate-high fall risk; community ambulation may be difficult; cut-off for fall risk is typically ≥13.5 seconds
option_c: The test is invalid for individuals over 75 years
option_d: Results are only meaningful if compared to the 6-minute walk test
rationale: The TUG test cut-off for fall risk in older adults is typically ≥13.5 seconds (some sources use 12 seconds). A score of 16 seconds indicates elevated fall risk and suggests impaired functional mobility. Scores >20 seconds suggest the patient may require assistance for most activities of daily living. The TUG is valid and widely used in older adults.

question_text: A 10-year-old child with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy is classified as GMFCS Level III. What does this indicate about their functional mobility?
option_a: Walks without limitations in any environment
option_b: Walks using a hand-held mobility device indoors; may use wheeled mobility outdoors or in the community
option_c: Self-mobility with wheeled mobility devices only
option_d: Transported in a manual wheelchair; has minimal self-mobility
rationale: GMFCS Level III: Children walk using a hand-held mobility device (walker, forearm crutches) in most indoor settings. They may transfer independently. For outdoor or community distances, they often use wheeled mobility. Level I = walks without limitations; Level II = walks without devices but limited in community; Level IV = self-mobility with powered device; Level V = transported.

question_text: A physiotherapist is treating a 25-year-old male athlete for an acute hamstring strain (Grade II). On day 7, the patient is pain-free at rest. Which phase of rehabilitation is MOST appropriate to begin?
option_a: Immediate return to full sport training with no restrictions
option_b: Progressive eccentric loading (e.g., Nordic hamstring curls, Romanian deadlifts) at sub-maximal intensity, ensuring pain-free exercise
option_c: Aggressive stretching to maximum range to break down adhesions
option_d: Continue complete rest for a further 2 weeks
rationale: By day 7 post-Grade II hamstring strain, when pain-free at rest, progressive eccentric loading (Nordic curls, RDLs) at sub-maximal intensities is appropriate and supported by evidence (including the Oslo protocol and Askling's L-protocol). Early progressive loading reduces re-injury risk and hastens return to sport. Aggressive stretching risks re-tear; extended rest leads to strength loss and delayed recovery.

question_text: A 35-year-old female runner presents with insidious onset lateral knee pain that worsens running downhill and at 30 minutes into a run. The Noble compression test is positive. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Lateral meniscus tear
option_b: Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS)
option_c: Proximal tibiofibular joint instability
option_d: Common peroneal nerve entrapment
rationale: Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS) presents with lateral knee pain typically at 30–40 minutes into a run (the 'impingement zone'), worsened by downhill running, and positive Noble compression test (pain reproduced with compression over the lateral femoral epicondyle at 30° knee flexion). Lateral meniscus tears typically have joint line tenderness and positive McMurray's. ITBS is the most common overuse injury in runners.

question_text: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of injury in a FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand) causing a distal radius fracture (Colles' fracture)?
option_a: Forced wrist flexion causing a volar plate rupture
option_b: Forced wrist dorsiflexion and radial deviation at impact, causing dorsal displacement of the distal radius fragment
option_c: Axial compression through a clenched fist causing a metacarpal fracture
option_d: Rotational force through the forearm causing a Galeazzi fracture
rationale: A Colles' fracture occurs when a fall on outstretched hand forces the wrist into dorsiflexion. The distal radius fractures with dorsal displacement and angulation, producing the classic 'dinner fork' deformity. It is the most common fracture in older adults, particularly postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Volar displacement characterizes a Smith's fracture.

question_text: A physiotherapist assessing a patient with suspected carpal tunnel syndrome performs the Phalen's test. What constitutes a POSITIVE result?
option_a: Pain reproduced in the anatomical snuffbox with wrist compression
option_b: Reproduction of tingling, numbness, or pain in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger) within 60 seconds of sustained wrist flexion
option_c: Pain along the ulnar border of the hand during wrist flexion
option_d: Loss of grip strength with sustained wrist extension
rationale: Phalen's test is performed by holding the wrists in full flexion for 60 seconds. A positive result is reproduction of symptoms (tingling, numbness, paresthesia, pain) in the median nerve distribution: thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger. Ulnar border symptoms suggest ulnar nerve involvement. Anatomical snuffbox tenderness is a sign of scaphoid fracture.

question_text: A 50-year-old male is 3 months post-C6 complete spinal cord injury (AIS A). Which functional outcome is REALISTIC to expect with maximal rehabilitation?
option_a: Independent ambulation with bilateral knee-ankle-foot orthoses
option_b: Independent manual wheelchair propulsion on level surfaces and pressure relief using wrist extensors; independence in some ADLs using tenodesis grip
option_c: Full independence in all ADLs without any assistive devices
option_d: Dependence for all mobility requiring a power wheelchair permanently
rationale: C6 complete SCI (AIS A): key preserved muscles include wrist extensors (ECRL/ECRB). With intact wrist extension, tenodesis grip is functional for light ADLs. Manual wheelchair independence on level surfaces is achievable. Ambulation is not a functional goal for complete C6 SCI. Power wheelchair may supplement for long distances but is not the only option. Full ADL independence is unrealistic without hand function.

question_text: During a stroke rehabilitation session, a patient is asked to reach for a cup and demonstrates mirror movements in the unaffected hand. This phenomenon is BEST explained by:
option_a: Bilateral cortical reorganization with intact corticospinal pathways causing involuntary contralateral motor overflow
option_b: Malingering — the patient is not trying to use only the affected hand
option_c: Severe spasticity preventing independent limb use
option_d: Peripheral nerve injury in the unaffected extremity
rationale: Mirror movements (synkinesis) after stroke result from abnormal bilateral activation of motor cortex during attempted unilateral movement, with motor commands overflowing to the contralateral limb through preserved or aberrant corticospinal pathways. This is a neurological phenomenon related to cortical reorganization, not malingering or spasticity. It is targeted in rehabilitation with constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT).

question_text: A 50-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy presents for post-myocardial infarction cardiac rehabilitation. Which additional screening is MOST important before initiating exercise?
option_a: Screen for autonomic neuropathy, which may blunt heart rate and blood pressure responses to exercise and mask anginal symptoms
option_b: Screen for retinopathy only, as this is the primary diabetes complication affecting exercise
option_c: No additional screening is needed beyond standard cardiac rehab intake
option_d: Defer all exercise until HbA1c is below 7%
rationale: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy (DAN) affects the cardiovascular autonomic nervous system, causing resting tachycardia, exercise intolerance, orthostatic hypotension, and — critically — silent ischemia (atypical or absent anginal symptoms). Patients with DAN may not report chest pain during myocardial ischemia, making objective monitoring (ECG, BP) essential. This is the most important additional screening consideration in this patient.

question_text: A 42-year-old woman is 8 weeks post total knee arthroplasty (TKA). She has ROM of 0-95° and has been walking with a cane. What is the PRIMARY functional milestone that determines readiness for stair climbing training?
option_a: Passive knee flexion of at least 120°
option_b: Sufficient quadriceps strength (MMT ≥4/5) and single-leg stance stability on the operated limb to control descent safely
option_c: Return to full pre-operative weight
option_d: Absence of any swelling in the knee
rationale: Stair climbing, especially stair descent (step-down), requires eccentric quadriceps control and single-limb stance stability on the operated limb. These are the primary prerequisites for safe stair training post-TKA. While ROM of 90-95° is needed for stair climbing, quadriceps strength (MMT ≥4/5) and the ability to control the body weight eccentrically on one limb are the critical safety factors.

question_text: In McKenzie mechanical diagnosis and therapy (MDT), a patient who demonstrates 'centralization' of symptoms during repeated lumbar flexion exercises is BEST managed by:
option_a: Avoiding all lumbar flexion and strictly using extension exercises
option_b: Continuing directional preference exercises in flexion, as centralization indicates a favorable response and pain moving from the periphery toward the spine predicts good outcomes
option_c: Immediate surgical referral as centralization indicates disc herniation requiring decompression
option_d: Switching to a completely different treatment approach, as centralization is a poor prognostic sign
rationale: Centralization in MDT refers to the progressive movement of distal referred pain toward the spine (midline) with repeated movements in a specific direction. It is a POSITIVE prognostic indicator and identifies the directional preference. When centralization occurs with flexion, the patient's directional preference is flexion, and continued flexion exercises are the appropriate treatment. Centralization predicts good outcomes with conservative MDT.

question_text: A physiotherapist is conducting a clinical prediction rule (CPR) assessment for a patient with suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT) using the Wells criteria. Which combination of findings gives a HIGH pre-test probability score requiring urgent imaging?
option_a: Calf tenderness only, with no swelling or risk factors
option_b: Active cancer, calf swelling >3 cm compared to asymptomatic side, localized tenderness along deep venous system, and recent immobilization
option_c: Varicose veins, minimal ankle swelling, and prior DVT 10 years ago
option_d: Superficial phlebitis without limb swelling
rationale: The Wells DVT score assigns points for: active cancer (+1), paralysis/plaster immobilization (+1), bedridden >3 days or major surgery in 12 weeks (+1), localized deep vein tenderness (+1), entire leg swelling (+1), calf swelling >3 cm (+1), pitting edema (+1), previous DVT (+1), alternative diagnosis less likely (+2). A score ≥3 = high probability. Option B includes multiple high-scoring criteria warranting urgent duplex ultrasound.

question_text: A 28-year-old male presents with morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes, buttock pain alternating sides, and bilateral sacroiliac joint tenderness. FABER test is positive bilaterally. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and the MOST appropriate physiotherapy approach?
option_a: Mechanical low back pain; extension-based McKenzie exercises
option_b: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) / axial spondyloarthropathy; education, aerobic exercise, spinal mobility exercises, and posture training
option_c: Bilateral hip osteoarthritis; joint mobilization and hip strengthening
option_d: Lumbar spinal stenosis; stationary cycling and lumbar flexion exercises
rationale: The presentation — young male, prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour), alternating buttock pain, bilateral SIJ tenderness, positive bilateral FABER — is classic for ankylosing spondylitis/axial spondyloarthropathy. The ASAS-EULAR guidelines recommend supervised exercise (aerobic, spinal mobility, posture), hydrotherapy, and patient education as first-line physiotherapy. NSAIDs and biologics are medical management.

question_text: A therapist uses the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) to assess spasticity in a stroke patient's elbow flexors. The examiner notes a 'catch' during passive movement followed by minimal resistance through the remainder of the range. What is the MAS score?
option_a: MAS 0 (no increase in muscle tone)
option_b: MAS 1 (slight increase, catch or minimal resistance at end of range)
option_c: MAS 1+ (slight increase, catch followed by minimal resistance through <50% of range)
option_d: MAS 2 (marked increase in tone through most of range, limb easily moved)
rationale: Modified Ashworth Scale: 0 = no increase; 1 = slight increase, catch or minimal resistance at end of range; 1+ = slight increase with a catch followed by minimal resistance through less than half the remaining ROM; 2 = marked increase but limb easily moved; 3 = considerable increase, passive movement difficult; 4 = rigid in flexion or extension. A catch with minimal resistance through the remainder of range = MAS 1+.

question_text: A physiotherapist is treating a 55-year-old male who is 5 days post-aortic valve replacement surgery. During ambulation, he develops sudden onset of right calf pain and swelling. His HR increases from 80 to 102 bpm. What is the MOST appropriate IMMEDIATE action?
option_a: Continue ambulation and reassess in 30 minutes
option_b: Stop the session immediately, return the patient to bed, notify the nursing staff and physician, and document findings — DVT must be ruled out
option_c: Apply ice to the calf and elevate the leg, then resume the ambulation session
option_d: Perform a Homan's sign test and proceed based on the result
rationale: Acute unilateral calf pain and swelling in a post-cardiac surgery patient with tachycardia requires immediate cessation of the session, bed rest, and urgent medical notification to rule out DVT and pulmonary embolism. DVT is a serious post-surgical complication. Continuing exercise risks embolization. Homan's sign is unreliable and discouraged. Ice and elevation do not address the underlying risk.

question_text: A therapist is assessing a chronic wound using the PUSH tool (Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing). Which three parameters does the PUSH tool measure?
option_a: Wound depth, wound odor, and wound pain level
option_b: Wound area (length × width), tissue type (necrotic/slough/granulation/epithelial), and exudate amount
option_c: Wound pH, biofilm presence, and wound temperature
option_d: Wound color, periwound skin condition, and wound undermining
rationale: The PUSH tool (Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing) scores three parameters: (1) wound area (length × width in cm²), (2) exudate amount (none/light/moderate/heavy), and (3) surface tissue type (necrotic tissue, slough, granulation tissue, epithelial tissue, or closed). A total score of 0 indicates a healed wound. It is a validated, simple tool for tracking pressure injury healing trajectory.

question_text: A 17-year-old female gymnast presents with insidious onset anterior knee pain worsened by squatting and stair descent, with patellar facet tenderness. Patellar grind test is positive. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and the MOST important component of rehabilitation?
option_a: Osgood-Schlatter disease; rest and bracing only
option_b: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS); hip strengthening (gluteus medius and external rotators) combined with quadriceps strengthening in pain-free ranges
option_c: Patellar tendinopathy; eccentric decline squat protocol exclusively
option_d: ACL tear; MRI and surgical referral
rationale: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) presents with anterior knee pain worse with squatting, stairs, prolonged sitting, and positive patellar facet tenderness and patellar grind test. Evidence-based rehabilitation centers on hip strengthening (gluteus medius, external rotators) to reduce dynamic valgus and medial patellar stress, combined with VMO-targeted quadriceps strengthening. This approach has the strongest RCT evidence for PFPS.

question_text: A 45-year-old male cancer patient undergoing chemotherapy for colon cancer has a platelet count of 30,000/μL. Which exercise guideline is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Full unrestricted exercise including contact sports and high-intensity weight training
option_b: Exercise is contraindicated at platelet counts below 50,000/μL; limit to gentle ROM and walking only, avoiding contact sports and activities with fall/bleeding risk
option_c: No restrictions on exercise type regardless of platelet count
option_d: Defer all physical activity until chemotherapy is completed
rationale: ACSM/oncology rehab guidelines recommend: Platelets >100,000 = full activity; 50,000–100,000 = moderate exercise, avoid contact or high-impact activities; <50,000 = avoid activities with bleeding risk; <20,000 = exercise contraindicated (bed rest/ADLs only). At 30,000/μL, gentle ROM, walking, and low-risk activities are permitted, but contact sports, heavy resistance training, and fall-risk activities are contraindicated.

question_text: Which gait deviation is MOST commonly observed in a patient with L4 nerve root weakness (weakness of tibialis anterior) after lumbar disc herniation?
option_a: Trendelenburg gait (hip drop toward the swing limb)
option_b: Steppage gait (excessive hip and knee flexion during swing to clear a dropped foot)
option_c: Scissor gait with hip adduction
option_d: Vaulting gait (rising on toe of stance limb to assist swing clearance on opposite side)
rationale: Weakness of tibialis anterior (L4 nerve root) causes foot drop — inability to dorsiflex the foot adequately during swing phase. To clear the foot, patients compensate with steppage gait (exaggerated hip and knee flexion during swing). Trendelenburg indicates weak hip abductors (gluteus medius, L5); scissor gait indicates spastic hip adductors (upper motor neuron lesion); vaulting compensates for swing clearance on the other side.

question_text: A 65-year-old woman with osteoporosis is referred for physiotherapy after a thoracic vertebral compression fracture (T8) without neurological deficit. Which exercise type should be AVOIDED in this patient?
option_a: Spinal extension strengthening exercises
option_b: Trunk flexion exercises (crunches, sit-ups, forward bending) that increase anterior vertebral body compressive loading
option_c: Walking and low-impact weight-bearing activities
option_d: Hip and lower extremity strengthening exercises
rationale: After thoracic vertebral compression fracture with osteoporosis, trunk flexion exercises (flexion-loading crunches, sit-ups, reaching forward) are contraindicated as they increase anterior column compressive forces on already-compromised vertebrae, risking further fracture. Spinal extension exercises are actually beneficial, building extensor muscle mass to unload vertebral bodies. Weight-bearing activity and lower extremity strengthening are encouraged.

question_text: A physiotherapist calculates a patient's MET (metabolic equivalent) level during exercise testing. What does 1 MET represent and at what MET level is a patient considered to have adequate functional capacity for most daily activities?
option_a: 1 MET = 2.0 mL O2/kg/min; ≥5 METs indicates adequate daily function
option_b: 1 MET = 3.5 mL O2/kg/min (resting oxygen consumption); ≥5 METs is considered adequate functional capacity for most daily activities
option_c: 1 MET = 1.0 mL O2/kg/min; ≥8 METs is required before returning to any activity
option_d: 1 MET = 3.5 mL O2/kg/min; ≥10 METs is required before cardiac rehab clearance
rationale: 1 MET = 3.5 mL O2/kg/min, representing resting metabolic rate. Most daily activities require 2–5 METs (light household tasks, slow walking ~3 METs; moderate work ~4-5 METs). A functional capacity of ≥5 METs is commonly cited as sufficient for most daily and light recreational activities. Patients <5 METs are considered to have poor functional capacity and higher cardiovascular risk.

question_text: A 30-year-old male rugby player sustains a shoulder dislocation (anterior glenohumeral dislocation) for the third time. On assessment, the anterior apprehension test is strongly positive. What is the PRIMARY rehabilitation goal and the likely long-term management consideration?
option_a: Passive rest for 8 weeks followed by return to sport with no specific rehabilitation
option_b: Surgical referral (Bankart repair or Latarjet procedure) given recurrent instability; pre-/post-surgical physiotherapy focuses on rotator cuff strengthening, proprioceptive training, and scapular stabilization
option_c: Sling immobilization for 6 weeks then return to sport
option_d: Steroid injection to reduce inflammation followed by immediate sport return
rationale: Recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation (3rd episode) in a young active male rugby player indicates significant structural instability (likely Bankart lesion and/or Hill-Sachs defect). Surgical management (Bankart repair or Latarjet for bone loss) is the recommended long-term solution given failure of conservative management with repeated dislocation. Physiotherapy is critical pre- and post-operatively.

question_text: During patient history taking, a 55-year-old man with low back pain reports night sweats, unintentional weight loss of 8 kg over 3 months, and a history of prostate cancer 4 years ago. What is the MOST appropriate action?
option_a: Begin a standard low back pain rehabilitation program as the symptoms are likely musculoskeletal
option_b: Recognize these as red flags for serious pathology (cancer metastasis); do not delay — refer urgently back to the physician for medical investigation
option_c: Prescribe thoracic spine mobilizations to address the thoracic component
option_d: Order a DEXA scan to rule out osteoporosis
rationale: Night sweats, unexplained weight loss >5% in 3 months, and a history of cancer are major red flags ('cancer alarm symptoms') for metastatic disease. Prostate cancer commonly metastasizes to the lumbar spine. This patient requires urgent medical referral and imaging (bone scan, MRI) to rule out spinal metastasis. Physiotherapy is contraindicated until serious pathology is excluded.

question_text: A physiotherapist is implementing constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) for a chronic stroke patient with a mildly affected arm. What is the MINIMUM motor criterion typically required for a patient to be a candidate for standard CIMT?
option_a: Full voluntary finger extension and wrist extension against gravity
option_b: At least 10° active wrist extension and 10° active finger extension (MCP joints) on the affected side
option_c: Brunnstrom Stage 6 motor recovery
option_d: No strength criteria — CIMT is appropriate for any level of upper limb function
rationale: Standard CIMT eligibility requires a minimum of 10° wrist extension and 10° extension of each finger (MCP joints) on the affected side — indicating sufficient voluntary motor control to benefit from intensive practice. Without this minimum, modified CIMT or other interventions are more appropriate. Full extension against gravity would be too high a threshold, excluding many potential beneficiaries.

question_text: A patient with lymphedema of the right arm following breast cancer treatment is assessed. Which is the CORRECT sequence of complete decongestive therapy (CDT) components?
option_a: Compression garment → exercise → skin care → manual lymphatic drainage (MLD)
option_b: Skin care → MLD → multi-layer compression bandaging → decongestive exercise
option_c: MLD → exercise → skin care → compression garment in that strict order
option_d: Exercise → MLD → skin care → no compression in the active phase
rationale: Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT) for lymphedema has two phases. In the intensive (Phase 1) phase, the components in order are: (1) Skin care (meticulous hygiene to prevent infection), (2) MLD (to redirect lymph), (3) Multi-layer compression bandaging (to maintain reduction between MLD sessions), and (4) Decongestive exercises (with bandaging in place). In the maintenance (Phase 2) phase, compression garments replace bandaging.

question_text: A 52-year-old male presents with bilateral buttock pain, lower extremity heaviness, and back pain that is relieved by leaning forward on a shopping cart. Standing increases symptoms; sitting relieves them. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Bilateral piriformis syndrome
option_b: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
option_c: Vascular claudication from peripheral arterial disease
option_d: Bilateral hip osteoarthritis
rationale: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis classically presents with bilateral lower limb heaviness/pain worsened by standing and walking (spinal extension narrows the spinal canal), relieved by sitting and forward flexion ('shopping cart sign' — leaning forward widens the canal). Vascular claudication is not posture-dependent and is relieved by stopping, not sitting/flexion specifically. Hip OA has groin pain and hip-specific signs.

question_text: A physiotherapist documents 'S' in a SOAP note. Which of the following CORRECTLY belongs in the 'S' (Subjective) section?
option_a: Goniometric measurement of knee flexion at 85°
option_b: Patient states: 'My knee pain is 6/10 today, worse on stairs than yesterday'
option_c: Patient demonstrates antalgic gait with reduced right stance time
option_d: Ultrasound applied at 1.0 W/cm² for 5 minutes to the patellar tendon
rationale: In SOAP documentation: S (Subjective) = what the patient reports (symptoms, pain rating, functional limitations in their words); O (Objective) = measurable findings (ROM, strength, observation, tests); A (Assessment) = clinical interpretation/diagnosis; P (Plan) = treatment plan. Patient-reported pain level and functional comparison to yesterday are subjective information. Goniometry, observed gait, and treatment parameters are objective.

question_text: Which incentive spirometry instruction is CORRECT for a post-abdominal surgery patient?
option_a: Exhale forcefully into the device as fast as possible 20 times per hour
option_b: After a normal exhalation, seal lips around mouthpiece, inhale slowly and deeply to raise the piston/float, hold 3-5 seconds at peak inspiration, then exhale normally; repeat 10 times per hour
option_c: Breathe rapidly in and out of the device for 2 minutes continuously
option_d: Use only while lying flat supine and avoid sitting upright during the exercise
rationale: Incentive spirometry technique: normal exhalation first → seal mouthpiece → slow deep inhalation to maximize piston/float elevation → hold 3-5 seconds at peak (plateau) → normal exhalation → repeat 10 repetitions per hour while awake. The slow sustained inhalation maximizes alveolar recruitment and prevents atelectasis. Slow deep breaths are more effective than rapid breathing; sitting upright (or semi-reclined) improves diaphragmatic excursion.

question_text: A physiotherapist applies joint mobilization to the lumbar spine using a Grade IV oscillation. According to Maitland's grading, what does Grade IV describe?
option_a: Small amplitude movement at the beginning of range, before resistance is encountered
option_b: Large amplitude movement through range up to the point of resistance
option_c: Small amplitude movement at the end of range into resistance/stiffness
option_d: Sustained stretch beyond the limit of range (manipulation/thrust)
rationale: Maitland's joint mobilization grades: Grade I = small amplitude at beginning of range; Grade II = large amplitude short of resistance; Grade III = large amplitude into resistance; Grade IV = small amplitude at end of range, into resistance/stiffness; Grade V = manipulation (high velocity thrust at end of range). Grade IV is used for pain-free stiffness and end-range restricted motion.

question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with facial droop, inability to raise her left eyebrow, and left-sided ear pain. Forehead sparing is NOT present. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Left central facial nerve palsy (UMN lesion — stroke)
option_b: Left peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy or LMN lesion) — involves the entire left face including the forehead
option_c: Right peripheral facial nerve palsy
option_d: Trigeminal neuralgia
rationale: A peripheral (LMN) facial nerve lesion (Bell's palsy) affects the ENTIRE ipsilateral face, including the forehead (forehead is NOT spared). A central (UMN) facial nerve lesion (e.g., stroke) spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical representation of forehead muscles. This patient has left-sided involvement without forehead sparing, indicating a left LMN (peripheral) lesion. Bell's palsy is the most common cause.

question_text: A 32-year-old female marathon runner presents with insidious onset anterior lower leg pain that is worse during and after running and slightly tender over the anterior-medial tibia. X-ray is normal. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and the INITIAL management?
option_a: Anterior compartment syndrome; emergency fasciotomy referral
option_b: Medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS/shin splints); relative rest, load modification, biomechanical assessment, gradual return to running program
option_c: Tibial stress fracture; immediate cessation of all weight-bearing and bone scan
option_d: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome; compartment pressure testing
rationale: Medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS) presents with diffuse anteriomedial tibial pain during/after running, with bony tenderness over a broad region of the tibia. X-ray is typically normal. Management: relative rest and load modification, correct biomechanical factors (overpronation, training errors), gradual return to running. Tibial stress fracture has more focal point tenderness; chronic exertional compartment syndrome resolves rapidly with rest and requires pressure testing for diagnosis.

question_text: A 48-year-old female is post-lobectomy (right upper lobe) for non-small cell lung cancer. She is day 2 post-op with a right-sided pleural chest drain in situ. Which physiotherapy intervention is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Avoid all mobility until the chest drain is removed
option_b: Early mobilization (sitting to standing, short walks with nurse), deep breathing exercises, and cough assistance with incisional support — the chest drain does not contraindicate early mobility
option_c: Vigorous percussion and postural drainage over the right chest immediately
option_d: Incentive spirometry at maximum effort with breath holding for 30 seconds
rationale: Chest drains are NOT a contraindication to early post-thoracotomy mobilization. Evidence strongly supports early mobility (day 1-2 post-op) to prevent complications (atelectasis, pneumonia, PE). Patients walk while managing the drainage system. Deep breathing, supported cough, and early ambulation are the core post-thoracotomy physiotherapy interventions. Vigorous percussion over a recent thoracotomy site is inappropriate.

question_text: A 19-year-old female volleyball player presents with a 6-week history of anterior knee pain at the inferior pole of the patella, worsened by jumping and landing. Tenderness is specifically at the patellar tendon insertion. The VISA-P questionnaire score is 45/100. What is the MOST evidence-based treatment?
option_a: Patellar tendon corticosteroid injection followed by 6 weeks rest
option_b: Progressive tendon loading program (isometric exercises for pain management during season, then heavy slow resistance and eccentric program for tissue adaptation)
option_c: Immediate surgical tendon debridement given the 6-week history
option_d: Patellar taping exclusively with no exercise
rationale: Patellar tendinopathy management: VISA-P score of 45/100 indicates significant impairment. During season, isometric quad contractions provide immediate analgesic effect (Rio et al. 2015). For tissue adaptation, progressive heavy slow resistance loading (HSR) and eccentric loading (e.g., decline squat) have the strongest evidence (Kongsgaard et al.). Corticosteroid injection may provide short-term relief but is associated with worse long-term tendon outcomes. Surgery is not indicated at 6 weeks.

question_text: The Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA) is used to evaluate which aspect of post-stroke motor recovery?
option_a: Functional independence in activities of daily living
option_b: Motor impairment severity, sensory function, balance, joint range of motion, and pain following stroke
option_c: Cognitive function and aphasia severity
option_d: Spasticity specifically using a standardized pendulum test
rationale: The Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA) is a comprehensive, validated post-stroke impairment measure that evaluates: motor function (upper and lower extremity synergy patterns and voluntary movement), sensory function, balance, joint ROM, and joint pain. The motor subscale (FMA-UE and FMA-LE) is most commonly used. It is not an ADL measure (that would be FIM/Barthel) nor a cognitive measure.

question_text: Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT/VAC therapy) is MOST indicated for which type of wound?
option_a: Superficial partial-thickness burns covering <5% TBSA
option_b: Large, complex wounds with significant depth such as open abdominal wounds, dehisced surgical wounds, or complex diabetic foot ulcers with adequate blood supply
option_c: Wounds with exposed untreated osteomyelitis
option_d: Dry, fully epithelialized wounds requiring moisture management
rationale: NPWT is most indicated for large complex wounds requiring: promotion of granulation tissue, reduction of edema/exudate, wound contraction, and maintenance of a moist environment. Ideal for open abdominal wounds, surgical dehiscence, complex diabetic ulcers with adequate perfusion, and large cavity wounds. Contraindications: untreated osteomyelitis (A), malignancy in wound, fistulae to organs/body cavities, dry/eschar wounds without debridement.

question_text: A physiotherapist is working with a 16-year-old male with an intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder. Which communication strategy is MOST appropriate to facilitate participation in therapy?
option_a: Use complex verbal instructions with detailed anatomical explanations
option_b: Use simple, concrete language with consistent routine, visual supports (pictures, demonstration), reduced verbal instructions, and allow processing time between instructions
option_c: Ignore behavioral challenges and proceed with therapy as planned
option_d: Always have a parent speak for the patient without direct communication
rationale: For patients with intellectual disability and ASD, best practices include: simple concrete language, predictable routine, visual supports (visual schedules, pictures, demonstrations), reduced verbal load with pauses for processing, positive reinforcement, and sensory considerations. Always communicate directly with the patient, adapting the communication style. Caregiver involvement supplements but should not replace direct patient communication.

question_text: A 40-year-old male presents with lateral hip pain worsened by walking, lying on the affected side, and crossing legs. Tenderness is over the greater trochanter and the FABER test reproduces lateral hip pain. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Hip joint osteoarthritis
option_b: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteal tendinopathy/trochanteric bursitis)
option_c: Femoral neck stress fracture
option_d: L4-L5 disc herniation with lateral hip radiation
rationale: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) — encompassing gluteal tendinopathy and/or trochanteric bursitis — presents with lateral hip pain, greater trochanter tenderness, pain with lying on the affected side (compressive load), crossing legs (adduction loading), and prolonged walking. FABER reproducing lateral hip pain suggests peritrochanteric pathology. Hip OA presents with groin pain and reduced IR. Femoral neck stress fracture causes groin pain worsened by weight-bearing.

question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature that distinguishes an UPPER motor neuron (UMN) lesion from a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion?
option_a: Muscle atrophy and fasciculations
option_b: Hyperreflexia, spasticity, and a positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar response)
option_c: Decreased deep tendon reflexes
option_d: Flaccid paralysis with absent muscle tone
rationale: UMN lesions (brain, spinal cord above the motor neuron) cause: hyperreflexia, spasticity (velocity-dependent hypertonia), clonus, positive Babinski sign, and minimal atrophy. LMN lesions (anterior horn cells, nerve roots, peripheral nerves) cause: hyporeflexia or areflexia, flaccid paralysis, significant muscle atrophy, and fasciculations. These distinctions are fundamental to neurological localization.

question_text: A 62-year-old woman with primary pulmonary hypertension (WHO Group I, PAH) is referred to physiotherapy. Which exercise prescription principle is MOST important to apply?
option_a: Maximize exercise intensity to improve pulmonary vascular remodeling as quickly as possible
option_b: Low-to-moderate intensity supervised exercise, avoiding isometric exercises and heavy resistance training; monitor for desaturation and symptoms closely; stop if SpO2 <88% or symptoms emerge
option_c: Exercise is absolutely contraindicated in all PAH patients
option_d: High-intensity interval training is the only effective modality for PAH
rationale: In pulmonary arterial hypertension, exercise rehabilitation is now recognized as beneficial but must be low-to-moderate intensity and closely supervised. Isometric exercise and heavy resistance training significantly increase right heart afterload and are avoided. SpO2 monitoring is essential; exercise stops if SpO2 <88% or if the patient develops syncope, severe dyspnea, or chest pain. Exercise is NOT absolutely contraindicated but requires expert supervision.

question_text: A 38-year-old female yoga instructor presents with anterior groin pain worsened by hip flexion, end-range rotation, and prolonged sitting. FADIR test is positive. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Inguinal hernia
option_b: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) — cam, pincer, or combined
option_c: Adductor strain
option_d: Iliotibial band tightness
rationale: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) presents with anterior groin/hip pain, positive FADIR test (Flexion-ADduction-Internal Rotation reproduces groin pain), worsened by deep hip flexion, prolonged sitting, and rotation activities. It is common in young athletic individuals and yoga practitioners with extreme hip ROM demands. Adductor strain causes pain with resisted adduction; inguinal hernia pain is typically reproduced with Valsalva.

question_text: Under the Canadian Physiotherapy Association's Code of Ethics, a physiotherapist discovers a colleague is providing treatments outside their competency, potentially causing patient harm. What is the physiotherapist's PRIMARY ethical obligation?
option_a: Ignore the situation to avoid workplace conflict
option_b: Address the situation through appropriate channels — first discussing with the colleague, then escalating to the clinic manager, professional organization, or regulatory body if the concern is not resolved, to protect patient safety
option_c: Immediately inform the patient and advise them to sue the colleague
option_d: Document the concern in the patient's chart without any further action
rationale: The CPA Code of Ethics and provincial regulatory standards require physiotherapists to act in the best interests of patient safety. This includes a duty to report concerns about unsafe or incompetent practice through appropriate mechanisms: first to the colleague (if safe to do so), then to management, and if unresolved, to the regulatory college/body. Patient safety is the paramount obligation. Ignoring or taking punitive direct action are both inappropriate responses.

question_text: A 55-year-old male with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) ALSFRS-R score of 32/48 is seen for physiotherapy. Which intervention is MOST appropriate at this stage?
option_a: High-intensity strengthening to maximize residual muscle mass
option_b: Moderate resistance and aerobic exercise within fatigue tolerance, energy conservation strategies, adaptive equipment prescription, and advance care planning discussion
option_c: No physiotherapy as ALS is a terminal diagnosis
option_d: Aggressive stretching to prevent all contractures regardless of comfort
rationale: ALS physiotherapy at moderate disease stage (ALSFRS-R 32 — moderately impaired) includes: moderate-intensity exercise within fatigue tolerance to maintain function, energy conservation, fall prevention, adaptive equipment and assistive technology prescription, and discussions about future care needs. High-intensity exercise risks overwork weakness in ALS. Physiotherapy provides significant quality of life benefit throughout the disease course.

question_text: Which bacterial organism is MOST commonly associated with infected pressure injuries in hospitalized patients and is of particular concern due to antibiotic resistance?
option_a: Streptococcus pyogenes
option_b: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
option_c: Haemophilus influenzae
option_d: Streptococcus pneumoniae
rationale: MRSA is the most clinically significant antibiotic-resistant organism in infected pressure injuries and chronic wounds in hospital and long-term care settings. MRSA biofilm formation makes these wounds particularly difficult to treat. Contact precautions and wound culture-guided antibiotic selection are essential. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is another important Gram-negative pathogen in pressure injuries, but MRSA is the primary concern for resistance.

question_text: A 70-year-old male with bilateral knee OA is assessed using the WOMAC (Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index). The WOMAC measures:
option_a: Radiographic joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation
option_b: Pain, stiffness, and physical function limitations specifically related to hip and knee osteoarthritis (self-report questionnaire)
option_c: Health-related quality of life across multiple body systems
option_d: Lower extremity muscle strength using dynamometry
rationale: The WOMAC is a validated, disease-specific self-report questionnaire for hip and knee osteoarthritis measuring three subscales: pain (5 items), stiffness (2 items), and physical function (17 items). Higher scores indicate worse outcomes. It is widely used as a primary outcome measure in OA clinical trials and rehabilitation. It does not measure radiographic changes or strength directly.

question_text: Which finding on auscultation is MOST consistent with a left-sided pleural effusion?
option_a: Fine late-inspiratory crackles bilaterally at the bases
option_b: Decreased/absent breath sounds at the left base with dullness to percussion
option_c: Wheeze throughout the left lung field on expiration
option_d: Bronchial breath sounds and increased tactile fremitus at the left base
rationale: Pleural effusion causes: decreased or absent breath sounds over the effusion (fluid blocks sound transmission), stony dullness to percussion (fluid), and reduced tactile/vocal fremitus. Bronchial breath sounds and increased fremitus are signs of consolidation (pneumonia). Fine late-inspiratory crackles suggest pulmonary edema or fibrosis. Wheeze indicates airway obstruction.

question_text: A physiotherapist is planning a randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing two exercise programs for chronic low back pain. Which level of evidence does a well-conducted RCT represent in the hierarchy of evidence?
option_a: Level V (expert opinion)
option_b: Level II (well-conducted RCT), just below systematic reviews/meta-analyses of RCTs (Level I)
option_c: Level III (non-randomized controlled study)
option_d: Level IV (case series)
rationale: Evidence hierarchy: Level I = systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs; Level II = individual well-conducted RCTs; Level III = non-randomized controlled studies, cohort studies; Level IV = case-control studies, case series; Level V = expert opinion, case reports. A well-conducted RCT (Level II) is strong evidence and is considered the gold standard for individual study designs testing intervention efficacy.

question_text: A 26-year-old female presents with wrist pain, clicking, and instability following a fall. Stress testing reveals laxity with the scaphoid shift test (Watson's test) positive. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
option_b: Scapholunate ligament instability
option_c: Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear
option_d: Carpal tunnel syndrome
rationale: Watson's test (scaphoid shift test) is specific for scapholunate ligament instability. A positive test produces a palpable/audible clunk and pain at the dorsal scaphoid as the scaphoid subluxes. Scapholunate instability is the most common carpal instability, often following a FOOSH. TFCC tears cause ulnar-sided wrist pain; De Quervain's is radial-sided tendinopathy; CTS is a compressive neuropathy.

question_text: A 67-year-old man with vestibular neuritis presents with persistent dizziness, gaze instability, and positive head impulse test (HIT) to the right. Which physiotherapy approach is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Complete bed rest for 6 weeks to allow the vestibular system to recover
option_b: Avoid all head movement exercises as they will worsen the vestibular lesion
option_c: Canalith repositioning maneuver (Epley's) for all vestibular complaints
rationale: Vestibular neuritis causes unilateral peripheral vestibular hypofunction. The head impulse test positive to the right indicates right-sided hypofunction. Management: vestibular rehabilitation (gaze stabilization/VOR exercises, habituation exercises, balance training) to promote central compensation — this is the most effective evidence-based intervention.
