Canalith repositioning (Epley's) is for BPPV, not vestibular neuritis. Rest delays compensation.

question_text: A patient on mechanical ventilation in the ICU has PEEP set at 8 cmH2O and FiO2 at 0.50. Which physiotherapy activity is GENERALLY contraindicated in the ICU setting?
option_a: Passive range of motion exercises to prevent contracture
option_b: Percussive chest physiotherapy to the face and neck region
option_c: Head-of-bed elevation to 30–45°
option_d: In-bed cycling with legs for mechanically ventilated patients
rationale: Percussive chest physiotherapy to the face, neck, or head is always contraindicated. In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, physiotherapy (passive ROM, head-of-bed elevation, in-bed cycling, positioning, early mobilization) is increasingly supported by evidence for preventing complications. However, standard chest physiotherapy (percussion/vibration) is generally not indicated for the face/neck region at any time and is inappropriate over intravascular lines or unstable areas.

question_text: A 50-year-old male presents with pain, swelling, and warmth in the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The attack began suddenly overnight. He reports a diet rich in red meat and alcohol. Serum uric acid is elevated. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and the physiotherapy role?
option_a: Rheumatoid arthritis; start aggressive joint mobilization immediately
option_b: Gout (hyperuricemia with monosodium urate crystal deposition); physiotherapy during the acute phase is limited to rest and cryotherapy; longer term: education on dietary modification, footwear advice, and general exercise
option_c: Septic arthritis; apply moist heat and begin weight-bearing exercises
option_d: Osteoarthritis; prescribe high-impact exercise to strengthen surrounding muscles
rationale: Gout in the first MTP joint (podagra) presents with sudden severe pain, erythema, swelling, and warmth, triggered by dietary purines and alcohol, with elevated uric acid. During acute flare, physiotherapy focuses on rest, elevation, and cryotherapy (ice). Active mobilization during an acute attack is contraindicated. Long-term, physiotherapy contributes through lifestyle education, footwear advice, and non-pharmacological management.

question_text: A physiotherapist wants to measure the minimal detectable change (MDC) for the 6-Minute Walk Test in a heart failure population. The MDC is BEST defined as:
option_a: The smallest difference in score that patients perceive as important and meaningful to them
option_b: The smallest change in score that exceeds measurement error (at a specified confidence level), indicating real change beyond chance
option_c: The average change seen in the intervention group of a randomized controlled trial
option_d: The difference between the 6MWT score and age-predicted normal values
rationale: The Minimal Detectable Change (MDC) is a statistical concept representing the smallest score change that exceeds measurement error (beyond the threshold of random variation) at a specified confidence level (usually 90% or 95%). It is calculated from the standard error of measurement. This is distinct from the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID), which represents the smallest change perceived as meaningful by patients.

question_text: A 25-year-old female recreational runner has been diagnosed with a grade 1 medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain of the right knee. Which statement regarding MCL healing and rehabilitation is MOST accurate?
option_a: Grade 1 MCL sprains require surgical repair and 6 months of non-weight-bearing
option_b: Grade 1 MCL sprains (no joint line opening) heal predictably with conservative management — protected weight-bearing as tolerated, early ROM exercise, and progressive strengthening; return to sport expected in 1–3 weeks
option_c: All MCL sprains require 6 weeks in a hinged knee brace locked at 0° extension
option_d: MCL sprains never heal without surgery as the MCL has poor blood supply
rationale: The MCL has an excellent blood supply and heals well conservatively. Grade 1 (mild, no instability) MCL sprains have an excellent prognosis: weight-bearing as tolerated, early motion exercises (no prolonged immobilization), progressive strengthening, and return to sport in 1–3 weeks. Grades 2–3 may require bracing and longer recovery. Surgery is rarely indicated for isolated MCL injuries, even Grade 3.

question_text: A 45-year-old male is referred for vestibular assessment following a fall. The Dix-Hallpike test to the right produces a brief (15–30 second) rotational nystagmus with a latency of 2–5 seconds. What does this indicate and what is the appropriate treatment?
option_a: Central vertigo requiring urgent neuroimaging; no physiotherapy treatment appropriate
option_b: Right posterior semicircular canal BPPV; treat with the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver to the right
option_c: Bilateral BPPV; treat with bilateral Epley maneuvers simultaneously
option_d: Vestibular neuritis; begin VOR gaze stabilization exercises
rationale: Dix-Hallpike positive to the right with brief (15–30s), geotropic (toward affected ear) rotational nystagmus with 2–5 second latency, and fatigability with repeated testing is classic for right posterior canal BPPV — the most common type of BPPV. Treatment: Epley canalith repositioning maneuver to the right side. Central vestibular lesions produce persistent, direction-changing nystagmus without latency.

question_text: A physiotherapist is treating a 78-year-old woman in her home who is identified as being at risk for elder abuse. Which is the physiotherapist's MOST appropriate action?
option_a: Discuss concerns only with family members present in the home
option_b: Attempt to have a private conversation with the patient to assess safety; document findings objectively; report to the appropriate authority (adult protective services, public health authority) per provincial legislation if abuse is suspected
option_c: Do nothing unless the patient explicitly requests help
option_d: Immediately discharge the patient from physiotherapy to avoid involvement
rationale: Physiotherapists have professional and legal obligations regarding suspected elder abuse. Key steps: (1) Attempt to speak privately with the patient away from potential abusers; (2) Assess safety and wishes; (3) Document observations objectively; (4) Report to appropriate authorities per provincial legislation (mandatory reporting varies by province but professional ethics always require action). Discharging, ignoring, or discussing with the potential abuser are all inappropriate.

question_text: A 30-year-old male with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is in the acute phase and in the ICU on mechanical ventilation. Which physiotherapy intervention takes HIGHEST priority at this stage?
option_a: Aggressive progressive resistive strengthening to prevent muscle wasting
option_b: Passive range of motion exercises to all limbs, positioning to prevent pressure injuries and contractures, and splinting for at-risk joints
option_c: Ambulation training with parallel bars
option_d: Electrical stimulation to strengthen weakened muscles at maximum intensity
rationale: In acute GBS requiring mechanical ventilation, physiotherapy priorities are passive ROM to prevent contractures, careful positioning to prevent pressure injuries, and splinting of at-risk joints (ankles, wrists). Active and resistive exercise is contraindicated in the acute progressive phase as overwork may worsen outcomes. Ambulation is impossible on mechanical ventilation. High-intensity electrical stimulation is inappropriate acutely.

question_text: A physiotherapist performs auscultation and notes 'velcro crackles' — late-inspiratory, fine, non-clearing crackles bilaterally at the posterior lung bases. Which condition is MOST consistent with this finding?
option_a: Asthma during an acute exacerbation
option_b: Pulmonary fibrosis (interstitial lung disease)
option_c: Pneumothorax
option_d: Large mucus plug causing lobar collapse
rationale: Bilateral, fine, late-inspiratory, non-clearing crackles described as 'velcro-like' at the lung bases are the classic auscultation finding of pulmonary fibrosis/interstitial lung disease. These crackles result from sudden opening of fibrosed alveoli during inspiration. They do not clear with coughing (distinguishing them from secretion-related crackles). Asthma = expiratory wheeze; pneumothorax = absent breath sounds; mucus plugs = coarse early-inspiratory crackles.

question_text: A 48-year-old female accountant presents with neck pain and right arm paresthesia in a C7 dermatomal pattern (middle finger, dorsal forearm). Spurling's test reproduces arm symptoms. Which clinical sign would confirm C7 nerve root involvement?
option_a: Reduced biceps reflex on the right
option_b: Weakness of wrist flexors and finger extensors, with reduced or absent triceps reflex on the right
option_c: Weakness of deltoid and biceps on the right
option_d: Reduced brachioradialis reflex on the right
rationale: C7 nerve root: myotome = wrist flexors, finger extensors (extensor digitorum), and triceps; reflex = triceps (C7); dermatomal = middle finger. C5 myotome = deltoid, biceps; C6 myotome = wrist extensors, biceps; C6 reflex = brachioradialis. Positive Spurling's test reproducing arm pain in a C7 distribution, combined with triceps weakness and reduced triceps reflex, confirms C7 radiculopathy.

question_text: Which of the following BEST describes the concept of informed consent in physiotherapy practice in Canada?
option_a: Informed consent is only required before surgical procedures, not physiotherapy
option_b: Informed consent requires the therapist to provide the patient with information about the proposed treatment, risks, benefits, alternatives, and consequences of no treatment, and the patient must voluntarily agree without coercion — it is an ongoing process
option_c: Once a patient signs an intake form, consent is implied for all future treatments
option_d: Verbal consent is never legally valid; written consent is required for all physiotherapy procedures
rationale: Canadian healthcare law and physiotherapy professional standards require valid informed consent: the patient receives adequate information (treatment, risks, benefits, alternatives, consequences of refusal), understands it, is capable of deciding, and voluntarily agrees. Consent is an ongoing process — patients can withdraw at any time. Initial consent does not cover all future treatments automatically. Verbal consent is legally valid for many procedures (written is required for some regulated acts).

question_text: When using the Braden Scale to assess pressure injury risk, which combination of scores represents the HIGHEST risk patient?
option_a: Total score of 20 (sensory perception: 4, moisture: 4, activity: 4, mobility: 4, nutrition: 2, friction/shear: 2)
option_b: Total score of 9 (sensory perception: 1, moisture: 2, activity: 1, mobility: 1, nutrition: 2, friction/shear: 2)
option_c: Total score of 15 (borderline risk threshold)
option_d: Total score of 23 (maximum possible, no risk)
rationale: The Braden Scale ranges from 6 (highest risk) to 23 (lowest risk). Risk thresholds: ≤9 = very high risk; 10–12 = high risk; 13–14 = moderate risk; 15–18 = mild risk; 19–23 = no risk. A total score of 9 with low scores across all subscales represents the highest-risk patient. A score of 23 is near maximum (lowest risk). Score 20 is normal/low risk.

question_text: A 58-year-old female is diagnosed with right shoulder-hand syndrome (complex regional pain syndrome Type I / CRPS-I) following a right MCA stroke. Which physiotherapy approach is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Aggressive passive stretching of the right shoulder and hand three times daily
option_b: Graded motor imagery (GMI), mirror therapy, desensitization, stress-loading, and gentle active/active-assisted exercise within a pain neuroscience framework
option_c: Complete immobilization of the affected limb in a sling permanently
option_d: Deep tissue massage and aggressive joint mobilization to break down edema
rationale: CRPS-I (shoulder-hand syndrome post-stroke) management includes: graded motor imagery and mirror therapy (strong evidence), gentle stress-loading (weight-bearing, traction), sensory desensitization, pain neuroscience education, and progressive active exercise respecting pain limits. Aggressive passive stretching and deep tissue massage worsen CRPS. Immobilization perpetuates disuse. GMI/mirror therapy have the strongest evidence for cortical reorganization and pain reduction.

question_text: A 22-year-old elite female rower presents with RED-S (Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport). She has a low BMI, absent menstrual periods for 8 months (amenorrhea), and reports fatigue and stress fractures. Which physiotherapy intervention is MOST important?
option_a: Immediately prescribe high-volume training to restore fitness
option_b: Reduce training load immediately; educate about energy availability; coordinate with sports medicine, dietitian, and psychologist as part of a multidisciplinary approach; gradual, supervised return to sport only when medically cleared
option_c: Focus only on the stress fracture management and ignore the other symptoms
option_d: Prescribe calcium supplements and continue all training as planned
rationale: RED-S (formerly Female Athlete Triad) requires multidisciplinary management. Physiotherapy role: reduce training load (critical and immediate), educate the athlete, coordinate with dietitian (energy intake), sports medicine physician (bone health, hormonal status), and sports psychologist (eating behaviors). Return to sport is a graduated process requiring medical clearance. Continuing or increasing training in RED-S with amenorrhea and stress fractures risks serious harm including additional fractures.
